rv.q: Sheehy’s originality makes an evocative play unmissable.
The other actors are uniformly superb in a play that is by turns, convulsively funny, bleak and puzzling.

A year after her Olivier-nominated performance in Machinal, Sheehy’s transformative, vanity and cliche-free turn here underscores how damn good she is and hopefully permanently elevates her to leading-actor status.
McPherson himself skillfully directs a splendid ensemble from which two names have to be singled out.
The real magic here comes from the beautifully woven speeches McPherson gives his characters as they rebel against tedium, death, and the heavens.
I’m not sure it quite adds up, but it’s far more interesting than plenty of plays that do.
Everyone acquits him or herself with stylish understatement and there is a palpably tight-knit cohesion in the troupe which resonates to the far corners of the Old Vic auditorium.
It is a production that envelops you in the warmth and melancholy of rural Ireland, delivering a family drama that is as evocative as it is quietly magical.
It’s a frustrating play, always watchable, so nearly great, so nearly soaring, yet somehow held earthbound by the weight of its intent.
I can't say I was as moved by Air as I had hoped I might be, given McPherson'
That dog, like the play, is serviceable, but it's not quite all you were hoping for.
For the most part deeply satisfying yet Air refuses to land the way The Weir does.
McPherson's play is always watchable, always interesting, and — at a time when many playwrights simply repeat banalities — he gives us complex characters and he does have fascinating things to say.

Unfortunately, there's hardly anything visually or narratively engaging about Air, other than for Gregory Clarke's sound design and Ben McQuinn on associate music capturing a beautiful, gentle and fascinating ambience which is never really replicated in McPherson's writing and direction, making for a tiring slog of a show instead.

The work of an obviously skilled creator but lacking the requisite drive to really lock into its themes, Air fizzles at times with its own potential, but never truly bubbles over in this relaxed, sometimes-unfocused production.

cn.t: McPherson's first original play in 12 years divides critics. Some praise its mystical Chekhovian family drama and ensemble performances, while others find it mellow and mundane, lacking the emotional punch of his earlier work.
